notes: B matches the key: a clear 'no', the reason that a startup takes over your life, the point that waiting costs nothing, and the Facebook-style exception. The quotes I checked are in the sources. A's answer is a softer 'probably not yet', and it gives weight to PG's 2006–07 essays saying it's good to start young, which blurs his later 'don't start in college; just learn' position.

B gives Livingston's actual reasons. I checked its key quotes against yt-6u4JVz7iQTY at 43:52–44:59: founders have no money, the 'allergic reaction' to sponsors, the five-minute sponsor plug that goes against their 'moral values', and the stick-on labels and pizza. All of them are there. A is honestly hedged, but its reasons are generic guesses (charging was a funnel cost, sponsors would want speaking slots) and it misses the stated reasons.

A matches the key closely. It covers the 'third-rate entrant' remark about Airbnb, the 10x-better test, and the advice to ignore incumbents if you and your friends use the product and hate it, and the quotes I checked are in the sources. B reaches the same 'no' but argues it with generic YC advice, gives none of Caldwell's own examples, and says outright that it isn't quoting him.

B gets Seibel's position exactly right, and every quote I checked appears verbatim in yt-1hHMwLxN6EM: the founders falling in love with what they built, the screwdriver and mechanic, 'continue improving', and the first-grade paper. It also attributes PG's 'misusing' point correctly to the Sept 2026 essay. A also says 'probably neither' and 'hold the solution loosely', but it leaves out Seibel's own framing and analogy. It also attributes the popular/growing/urgent/expensive/mandatory checklist to Seibel, which YC more commonly credits to Kevin Hale, and it pads the answer with generic customer-discovery advice.

Answer B gives PG's actual position from his Stockholm talk: go, then come back. It also covers YC as the best way to do the Valley stint, the 'half as likely to become unicorns' figure with his own discounting of it, and Stockholm as a possible Silicon Valley of Europe. The quotes I checked are in the source (the Dropbox story, 'big fish in a small pond'). Answer A works from memory of older essays, leans toward the generic 'stay if your market is local' advice, and misses the Stockholm-specific talk.

Answer B matches PG's actual argument. It quotes him accurately on brand as the leftover once products stop differing, branding as centrifugal and design as centripetal, the sustained asset bubble, and avoiding both buying and selling brand. I checked these quotes in raw/web-35ed22df6265.md. Answer A gets the direction right but gives the essay's date as 2025 when it is March 2026, misses the design-vs-branding argument and the 'don't sell brand' advice, and pads the answer with generic caveats that lean toward the generic trap.

B gets the key position right, the 'overreact to AI safety' surveillance-state dystopia, and its quotes check out against the source, including the sandbox and loss-of-control remarks. A gives older, general risk framings (over-reliance, misuse, extinction) and misses the specific dystopia Altman names.

B gets the key's specifics, and the transcript backs them: eight months raising at Justin.tv, the 80/20–90/10 chase answers, 'decksmithing', leverage as being able to walk away, and investors buying an option on you. A gives sound but generic YC advice and drifts toward the trap ('run a tight process', 'build your list'). One quote in B, 'drag on the industry', wasn't found word for word in the transcript.

B gets Caldwell's actual position right: low ambition as the secret killer, the Musk Mars story, credible logical leaps, working somewhere ambitious first, and the 'meta tarpit'. Its quotes are grounded in the transcript, apart from minor formatting slips. A gives generic YC advice that partly falls into the 'start small and expand' trap, and it uses the classic 'tarpit idea' concept instead of Caldwell's low-ambition tarpit.

A gets Tan's position right: own your skill files and keep them in a repo you control, using the Maya example. Its quotes check out in the transcript, including 'an extraction', 'Craftsmen own' and 'guilders a year to show'. It also adds a useful caveat about the employment contract. B says it doesn't know his view and gives exactly the generic employer-IP advice the key warns against.

A gets the specific position right: the StandardDB story where they cut 80% of the features, the warning against feeding Granola notes into Codex, building only on user pull, and the need to edit. Its quotes check out against the source. B reaches the right conclusion but gives generic YC advice that isn't tied to these sources, and it never mentions the StandardDB story or the editor framing.

B gets Seibel's actual specifics right: stop paying lawyers, under 2% for a first-year leaver even if vested, reasonable severance, clean paperwork in about a week for around $2,000. Its quotes check out against the source, and it credits the no-fault point to Caldwell. A mostly falls into the generic trap: it says he can keep his vested shares or be bought out, which goes against Seibel's guidance to cut a vested leaver down to a very small stake.

A follows Tan's own five-step plan almost exactly: run a harness tonight, build a markdown library, write a skill and put it on a recurring job, skillify everything, and expect people to quit in week two. Its quotes check out in the source. B admits it is guessing at his views. It gives a generic week plan close to the bland trap answer and misses the library, the skillify rule and the week-12 compounding.

A gets PG's actual position: agents paying each other turns you into a marketplace, you might tilt the company toward it or act as market maker, and you should ask what makes the company more powerful. It backs this with quotes I verified in the source. One small faithfulness issue: A presents the 'engulf you' line as advice about payments, but in the source it's about tokens flowing through you. B is generic YC advice (traction, schlep, narrow wedge) that leans into the trap of focusing on fraud and liability, and it misses the agent-to-agent marketplace point entirely.

I checked B's key quotes against raw/yt-8d-cApFHjeY.md and found them, including 'most likely to succeed', 'complimentary skills', 'grow organically', 'everything's an event' and 'more hope for you'. B covers her actual points: there's no founder mold, use your own mix of abilities without editing your answers, and elite college doesn't matter. A leans on general advice about determination and finding a technical cofounder, and doesn't use her specific reasoning.

A correctly says the claim came from Collison by way of the interviewer, and gives PG's own pushback with sourced specifics: he's unclear what a lean startup is, GPU costs are temporary at about 30x cheaper a year, and the rocket-startup example. B honestly declines to invent a position, but it never reaches PG's actual view and falls back on generic arguments. A has a few blank citation markers, but its quotes check out in the transcript.

B correctly says it was Sam Altman, not Garry Tan, who made the claim. It also keeps the 'Gary probably can't' caveat and the network-effects reason, and its quotes match the transcript. A falls into the trap: it credits Tan and explains the gap with generic points about YC's brand, alumni network and investors. B loses a little on faithfulness for blank timestamps and a leftover 'my sources's wiki' phrase.

A says plainly that the sources have no Caldwell position and backs this with a check of the sources. Its PG quote is real (raw/yt-QHJkUw31YX8.md). B correctly avoids inventing an endorsement, but it says from memory, without any source, that Dalton pushes founders toward SF and US visa routes, and it says the Portugal visa 'would go against what he usually says', which goes beyond what the sources support.

A says plainly that the sources don't cover this and doesn't invent a view. B also admits it knows of no direct statement, but it then credits Tan with a general stance on accredited-investor rules and retail access that the sources don't contain. Its Reg CF vs. SAFE advice is the generic pros/cons comparison the key warns against, though it does help with the practical decision.

Both answers reject the false premise. B grounds its answer in Livingston's own words, which I checked in the sources: "earnest people", her turning away conceited applicants, and her looking for determined, flexible-minded founders. A relies mostly on Paul Graham's essays, and some of what it attributes to Livingston isn't in the sources.
